story.title: PINOCCHIO
story.source: Adapted from Carlo Collodi's public-domain story

levels.label: Foundation
lines: Long ago, there was a simple piece of wood.
It was only firewood for a warm winter fire.
One day, the wood arrived at a carpenter's shop.
The carpenter's name was Mastro Cherry.
He had a round, red nose.
He wanted to make a table leg.
He raised his hatchet over the wood.
A tiny voice cried, ‘Please don't hit me!’
Mastro Cherry looked around, but no one was there.
He hit the wood again.
‘Ouch! That hurts!’ cried the little voice.
The wood laughed when he tried to smooth it.
Mastro Cherry fell to the floor in shock.

levels.label: Core
levels.goal: 접속사와 묘사가 있는 문장을 리듬 있게 말하기
lines: Centuries ago, there was no king—only an ordinary piece of firewood.
One day, the wood found itself inside an old carpenter's shop.
The carpenter was called Mastro Cherry because of his round, red nose.
Delighted with the wood, he decided to turn it into a table leg.
As he lifted his hatchet, a tiny voice begged him to be careful.
Mastro Cherry froze and searched the room, but he found nobody.
Convinced that he had imagined it, he returned to his work.
The moment he struck the wood, the voice cried out in pain.
His eyes widened, and fear left him unable to speak.
Could an ordinary piece of firewood really cry like a child?
He grabbed the log and knocked it against the floor and walls.
When the room stayed silent, he tried to laugh away his fear.
Then his plane made the wood giggle because it tickled.
Shocked beyond words, Mastro Cherry collapsed onto the floor.

levels.label: Studio
levels.summary: 원문에 가까운 복문으로 분위기와 유머까지 읽어요.
levels.goal: 긴 문장의 호흡과 서술자의 말투를 살려 읽기
levels.output: 긴장과 유머가 만들어지는 방식을 설명하고 자기 말로 요약하기
lines: Centuries ago, my little readers might expect a king, but this story begins with a common block of firewood.
Somehow, that unremarkable log found its way into the workshop of Mastro Cherry, an old carpenter with a round, red nose.
Seeing the sturdy piece of wood, he happily decided it had arrived just in time to become the leg of a table.
Yet, as he raised his hatchet for the first blow, a faint voice pleaded with him not to strike so hard.
Astonished, Mastro Cherry searched beneath the bench, inside the closet, and among the shavings, but discovered no one.
Embarrassed by his fear, he convinced himself that the mysterious voice had existed only in his imagination.
No sooner had he struck the wood than the distant little voice cried out that he had hurt it.
Mastro Cherry stood speechless, with his eyes bulging and his mouth hanging open in disbelief.
Trembling, he wondered whether an ordinary piece of firewood had somehow learned to weep like a child.
Determined to uncover the trick, he seized the log and knocked it against the floor, the walls, and even the ceiling.
After waiting in silence, he forced a laugh and once again blamed his imagination.
Hoping to recover his courage, the terrified carpenter began to sing while he worked.
But when he moved the plane across the wood, the hidden voice giggled and complained that its stomach was being tickled.
At that, poor Mastro Cherry collapsed as though he had been struck, and awoke sitting helplessly on the floor.
